items.title: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
items.summary: I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives. A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company.

items.title: Are the trades a safe career transition?
items.summary: I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement... Are the trades safe? Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off And if not the trades, then what is a better bet?

deep.body: I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement... Are the trades safe? Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off And if not the trades, then what is a better bet?

comments.text: I guess safe is a relative term. I've met a lot more 9 fingered mechanics than software developers. >jumping ship that sure seems unwise to throw away a position in a time of pre-supposed insecurity.
The only careers where you can have certainty about what will happen to your job after the robots are better than you are chess grandmaster and marathon runner.

They're making pretty good progress on hands[1,2], I don't have a good sense of how quickly these things will become cheap enough to become ubiquitous, I'd imagine > 5 years but Plummer is probably the safest of the trades if I had to guess. That said, I'd encourage you to think more about other things humans are likely to always want/need - see if any of the other options are interesting to you? For example, lots of people are and will continue to be lonely, having a bar to sit at with someone friendly/interesting is a tool we use for this (I wrote a blog post about this idea: https://b.h4x.zip/finale/ ) - but there are also things like undertakers, kids activities centers/camp councilor, etc. Not all of these things will be equally financially rewarding, but maybe you're able to think about rewarding in other ways.

I'd wait a bit before jumping ships, the future is always different from what people think it will be. If you are really worried, you can get some training in a different job right now and keep it as a plan B.

AI is definitely changing things a lot in the field, but don't discount the massive change in how cheap money was during ZIRP and how expensive it became after ZIRP finally ended. This was coincidentally around the same time the layoffs in big tech started, which was before AI really had any meaningful impact. When money is cheap it is a lot easier for companies to hire, and when money suddenly stops being cheap it is a lot harder. In particular, large discontinuities in economic conditions, which we just experienced recently post-covid, always produce downturns in affected industries (which is distinct from the first order aspect of how expensive money is). So I think even ignoring AI we could expect several years of down-ness and reorganization followed by a recovery. I don't think we can even tell this point if AI will reduce demand for developers.

Check the trades subreddits (hvac, plumbing, electric) - lots of people not being able to find jobs or get into apprenticeships. Words like "oversaturated". My feeling is that we're 5-10 years too late but it might vary by region.
I'm starting a new business called handjobs for billionaires. Gotta get with the K-shaped economy. We all just create luxury products for the ruling class now. Bend the knee or be left behind.

Trades are boom bust even more so than software engineering. There is a shortage, people run to the field, but by the time they are trained up (end of apprenticeship) there is probably a bust because there are too many people in them. You need to be prepared to sweat out at least one bust at the beginning of your career, and stay in it so you can reap a boom or two. It’s definitely an exciting time to be in robotics, though it looks like the Chinese are pushing more aggressively into it thsn western developed nations. AI is also a huge risk to the trades (the joke about the plumber just needing to know hit im a call means those quick calls are at risk because that knowledge is easy to get with a chat bot).

items.title: Where the company's employees launch the tools that Claude created
items.summary: Hi everyone, Here is a situation: In a typical company these days, many employees are creating tools using AI (Claude & Cursor) to help with their work. They run these tools on their own computers, which no one else can use or on a builder platform with a public URL and either no login or a hand-rolled one the agent wrote. Question: Where do they run this? Who can see it? What happens if an employee leaves the company?

items.title: Is prompt tuning still a thing today? Anybody still using the likes of DSPy?
items.summary: Just a random thought that came up when I was discussing AI engineering challenges with some folks. Prompt engineering/tuning was definitely "a thing" during the ChatGPT-3.5 era. There were all sorts of fancy rule of thumb people were advocating, as well as formal approaches like GEPA that were then incorporated into frameworks like DSPy which were also briefly popular. Having said that, it's been a while since I've come across conversations on this topic, which means it's either dead or it's already working well in production.

items.title: Is Anthropic being public better or worse for your org?
items.summary: Now that Anthropic has a "fiduciary duty to maximize shareholder value"*, have you or your org started thinking about what that means medium to long term? For example, if you are using their models in production or production-adjacent systems, how do price changes impact your business? * I know they have a complicated governing system, but at the end of the day they have different pressures now than when they were private.

deep.body: Now that Anthropic has a "fiduciary duty to maximize shareholder value"*, have you or your org started thinking about what that means medium to long term? For example, if you are using their models in production or production-adjacent systems, how do price changes impact your business? * I know they have a complicated governing system, but at the end of the day they have different pressures now than when they were private.

comments.text: I suspect they'll miss earnings, panic, raise costs and that will be worse for our org cost wise, but likely better in the long term if it results in less reliance.

I fully expect when push comes to shove, they will start to prioritize profit above all else. Realistically the current state is that everyone's claude usage is very likely being heavily subsidized in order to juice growth.

Well at some point they will try and start to ramp up prices, so long-term it might be detrimental. In general I think the reasoning of these companies is that a single developer costs 10,000-20,000 USD per month so if they can be 3-4x more productive then basically companies should be able to pay around 10,000-20,000 USD for tokens for one employee. Today that sounds insane though, so not sure if we will ever get there. And of course that only works if running equally powerful development models on your own hardware is constrained, foreign providers are banned and domestic providers collude on price. Expect them to work more agressively towards all three things happening. Alternatively they will work on expanding the scope of use for these models, you can already see that with ChatGPT that e.g. markets to small shop owners, house wives etc.
I think it is both as they claim that their AI will cure cancer

I expect them to slowly cannibalize other softwares and create an ecosystem which will enable them to sell a M365 style service. So, if a company doesn't have a good enough hook, they might be in threat. But Anthropic's growth obligations are unrealistic for the debt they have

> Now that Anthropic has a "fiduciary duty to maximize shareholder value" They don't. There may be shareholder expectations along those lines, and investors will make choices accordingly, but there is no fiduciary duty to do so.
